Case Study · Product Design · Premium Game PC/Console

PROJECT TOWER

PAX · Paris Games Week · Validated by Shuhei Yoshida, PlayStation Indie

50K wishlists. 3K sales. Not a failure to hide. A rigorous product diagnosis on a team of four, no publisher, no external funding. This case study documents why interest did not convert to purchase, what we did about it, and where the UX ceiling was.

RoleProduct Designer
PlatformsSteam & PS5
Team4 people, 0 publisher
EngineUnreal Engine 5

Industry validation

Played and validated by Shuhei Yoshida, then head of PlayStation Indie.

Selected at PAX Seattle, AG French Direct, MIX, PAX Rising Showcase. Supported by the PlayStation Indie team. Steam: Mostly Positive · PS Store: 3.94/5 (~1,300 ratings). Fully self-published.

Key Insight

Strong wishlist traction can mask a positioning problem rather than validate product-market fit. The question is not "did people like the game?" It is "did the promise match what they were willing to pay for?"

00 — Context

Visible.
Not convincing enough.

Project Tower is a narrative sci-fi third-person shooter with a morphing mechanic, built in Unreal Engine 5. Our team's first premium PC/console release, a step up from the hypercasual mobile model we knew.

My scope: UX, game design, onboarding, UI, environmental guidance, and reading Steam and player data to drive iterations.

The core problem

The game attracted attention. It did not convert it. And once players purchased, a portion dropped before experiencing the strongest parts. Two distinct problems requiring two different lenses.

What this case study is

A diagnosis of product constraints under real indie conditions and an honest account of where UX can help, and where it cannot.

01 — Diagnostic

Three problems.
One root cause.

Analysis drew from Steam data (wishlists, conversion, playtime), player reviews, and firsthand feedback from events. It pointed to three converging issues with one structural tension underneath all of them.

D1Conversion & perceived value

50KWishlists2-3%ConversionHighDeletions

Wishlist spikes correlated directly with exposure moments: PAX, Gamescom, TGS, PGW, and digital festivals. The game captured attention when shown. But that attention did not become purchase. On Steam, purchase decisions are fast and comparative.

Interest existed. Perceived value at the moment of purchase did not match the ask.
Wishlist activity — Steam dashboard

50,042 additions · 15,221 deletions · spikes correlated with events

D2Engagement erosion
57%
Quit around 1h
39%
Reach 2h
4h43
Avg playtime

Players do not drop immediately. The average of 4h43 on a 7h game shows real engagement. But the majority does not reach the end. Recurring friction: difficulty spike felt abrupt, shooting feedback perceived as low-impact, pacing gaps between intensity peaks.

The engagement problem is not just onboarding. It is sustained pacing, which UX can partially address but not fully solve.
Lifetime play time stats - Steam

57% quit around 1h · 39% reach 2h · avg 4h43 · 1,015 users measured

D3Promise vs reality gap

The visual direction positioned the game at near AA/AAA quality. That drove the 50K wishlists. But a team of four has real production constraints. Content density, enemy variety, and pacing consistency could not fully sustain that visual promise across the full run.

Structural limit

This gap between promise and delivery is the core tension. It cannot be solved by UX alone. It requires either more content or a repositioned marketing promise. Neither was within my scope.

02 — Process (Messy Middle)

What the work
actually looked like.

Before the clean interventions, there was a messier phase: collecting fragmented signals, forming hypotheses, running things that did not work, and narrowing down to what was worth building.

Player feedback — annotated signals

Steam review — negative

"The concept and gameplay are good, but everything changed once I got under water. The boss killed me 3-5 seconds into the cut scene ending without even using an attack."

→ Difficulty spike not telegraphed. Onboarding stops too early.

Steam review — mixed

"Control of the character under water felt ok, but its very sluggish. I still think the concept and gameplay are good."

→ Core loop appreciated. Execution friction in specific moments.

Event playtest — PAX floor

"Where do I go?" — most common question in first 3 minutes of Level 1.

→ Navigation failure before players engage with the game itself.

Event playtest — salon demo

Players consistently missed narrative dialogue during combat. Post-demo: "What's the story again?"

→ Narrative delivery broken by action pacing.

Hypotheses formed — kept vs dropped

Hypothesis A

Players fail early because they do not understand controls — add explicit tutorial screens.

✗ Dropped — breaks immersion. Replaced by in-context learning.

Hypothesis B

Confusion in Level 1 is a UI problem — add waypoints or map indicators.

✗ Dropped — adds visual noise. Replaced by environmental lighting guidance.

Hypothesis C

Narrative loss is a pacing problem — trigger dialogue in dedicated zones.

✓ Kept — significantly improved narrative comprehension.

Hypothesis D

HUD information overload contributes to cognitive friction in combat.

✓ Kept — reduced UI to essentials, confirmed in playtests.

03 — Interventions

Five changes.
One constraint.

Each intervention targeted a specific friction with maximum impact per production cost, improving legibility, comprehension, and guidance without touching the game's structure.

01Structured onboarding through gameplay

Problem

Players did not grasp controls or key mechanics in first minutes. Observed in events and demo sessions.

Decision

In-context learning: progressive mechanic introduction (shoot, jump, morph), deferred advanced mechanics, no dedicated tutorial screen.

Execution

Triggered teaching moments tied to level beats. Advanced mechanics held back until players demonstrated basic fluency.

Observed effect

Fewer navigation questions in demo sessions. Faster mechanic comprehension observed in playtests.

Learning to jump

Triggered in context, no tutorial screen

Learning to crouch

Deferred introduction, triggered when relevant

Players reached core gameplay faster with less confusion, without a single tutorial screen.
02Minimal UI — reduce cognitive load in combat

Problem

Original HUD displayed health, ammo, morph state, reload indicator, cluttering action readability.

Decision

Strip UI to essentials: health and morph state only. Shoot feedback integrated into crosshair. Ammo removed.

Execution

Crosshair carries all real-time feedback. Interface becomes a support layer, invisible unless needed.

Observed effect

Cleaner action readability in playtests. Less visual distraction reported.

Video — Simplified UI, ammo integrated into crosshair

Before: separate ammo and reload. After: all integrated into crosshair.

HUD elements on screen

Data · Stamina · Life · Morph Icon · Crosshair · Ammo · Reload · Morphing Button

UI became invisible infrastructure, present when needed, absent otherwise.
03Environmental guidance without UI

Problem

"Where do I go?" was the most common question in Level 1. Players got lost before engaging with the game.

Decision

Environmental lighting to highlight key zones. Contrast between primary paths and secondary areas. Natural sight lines to objectives.

Execution

Directed light sources toward objectives. Darkened dead ends and secondary spaces. No waypoints or map overlay added.

Observed effect

Navigation failures dropped in subsequent demo sessions. Players moved forward without asking for direction.

Environmental lighting guidance — 3 annotated zones

Light = direction · Green: main path · Red: blocked zones

Players guided implicitly, no immersion break, no UI overhead.
04Narrative pacing — structure dialogue delivery

Problem

Story dialogue triggered during action sequences. Players could not read subtitles while playing.

Decision

Trigger narrative moments in dedicated zones. Temporarily reduce player input during key dialogue. Remove competing distractions.

Execution

Designated narrative beats mapped to calm level sections. Subtle movement constraint during critical dialogue.

Observed effect

Improved subtitle reading and narrative recall in post-demo feedback.

Comprehension structured, not assumed.
05Hiks alphabet — environmental world-building

Problem

World felt generic in environmental details. No visual language specific to the Hiks civilization.

Decision

Design a fictional script for the Hiks. Integrate it into environment surfaces and interaction points.

Execution

Full alphabet designed and applied across Level 1 environments and interaction triggers.

Observed effect

Stronger world coherence. Attentive players noticed and engaged with the environmental narrative layer.

Hiks alphabet design system

Fictional writing system for the Hiks universe

Integrated as in-game texture

Interaction points and environments

The environment became a narrative layer, not just a backdrop.

What moved.
What did not.

Honest read

UX reduced friction and improved the existing experience. It could not compensate for the gap between what the game promised visually and what it delivered in content volume.

05 — What We Considered But Rejected

Four options
we did not take.

Good product decisions are not just about what you do. They are about what you choose not to do, and why.

A — Lower the price

Why considered

Reducing the price could lower the purchase barrier and improve conversion from the wishlist.

Why rejected

Price reduction would have signaled lower quality, not better value. Players were not declining because of price. The perceived value was not clear enough.

B — Add more content

Why considered

More levels, more enemies, more variety would directly address the content density gap.

Why rejected

A team of four has a hard production ceiling. We had already cut one full level to protect quality. Adding half-finished content would make the perception problem worse.

C — Reposition the marketing promise

Why considered

Repositioning toward a tighter indie experience would better match what the game actually delivers and reduce player disappointment.

Why rejected

This was the most strategically valid option. But it required reworking trailers, key art, and Steam page copy, bandwidth we did not have. It remains the most actionable lever for a future update.

D — Major gameplay rework

Why considered

Player feedback pointed to specific friction: difficulty spikes, low-impact shooting, pacing gaps.

Why rejected

Post-launch rework of core systems on a shipped game, with four people and no publisher. Not realistic.

06 — Trade-offs & Hard Calls

Knowing what
not to do.

On a premium project run by four people, you cannot treat everything simultaneously. These three decisions were the most consequential.

We cut an entire level.

One full level was removed during production. It had no significant narrative value, proposed a long but low-density experience, and required disproportionate production effort to polish. An experience that is shorter but controlled is better than one that is longer but uneven.

We prioritized onboarding over additional content.

Product data showed that the first hours of play determined retention, quality perception, and overall engagement. Resources went into onboarding, legibility, and progression fluidity, not additional content. Fixing the entry point has compounding returns.

We accepted the structural limits.

Some identified problems required structural changes incompatible with our resources or timeline. The approach: optimize what exists, reduce critical friction, accept that some limits are real product constraints.

07 — Learnings

What this project
taught me.

Strong traction does not validate product-market fit.

50K wishlists felt like confirmation. It was a positioning signal. People found the game interesting enough to save it. Converting that interest required something the visual promise was not fully delivering.

UX optimizes the experience. It does not replace product strategy.

Every intervention improved something real. None of them addressed the gap between visual promise and content reality. Recognizing where UX ends and product strategy begins is part of the job.

Cutting content is a product decision, not a failure.

Removing the level was the right call. It protected the quality of what remained. Shipping something underbaked because it was already built is a sunk cost fallacy.

Engagement does not only depend on the first hour.

Fixing onboarding improved early game metrics. But 4h43 average playtime on a 7-hour game means the problem extends well beyond entry. Sustaining pacing across a full run requires content depth UX alone cannot substitute for.

Designing under constraint means prioritizing impact, not effort.

Environmental lighting guidance had more impact per hour invested than any UI rework. The constraint forces clarity about what actually moves the needle.
